title: Users, groups, administrative accounts and UAC

videos.script: A new person starts at the office on Monday. She needs an account on the shared computer, access to her team's folder, and nothing more. Ana also needs to decide something she has put off. Every person in the office currently signs in as an administrator, because that was easier when the computers were set up. {{monday}} An administrator account can install anything, change any setting and read any file. That is convenient on the day you need it, and it is also what a malicious attachment gets when an administrator opens it. The fewer things that run with that power, the less a mistake can reach. {{power}} All three systems agree on the idea: people use ordinary accounts, and administrator power is borrowed for a moment and handed back. Linux does it with sudo, Windows with User Account Control, and macOS with a password dialog. {{borrow}} You will see where Linux keeps its accounts, and create, lock and remove one. You will see who may use sudo, and where every use is recorded. Then the same on Windows and macOS, and exactly what UAC asks and why. {{steps}} The Linux transcripts come from lesson 3's server, with one extra user created and removed for the lesson. The Windows and macOS commands are shown, not run. {{honest}}
